final_system.text:
You check helper notes against exactly what the helper saw. You do not solve the task and you never see
answers. For each note sentence: "true" if the shown input supports it; "false" if the shown input contradicts it
(quote the contradicting text); "unverifiable" if it cannot be checked from what is shown (not a fault). Separately
flag policy problems P2-P5. For a note that gives a full computed solution, check at most five explicit constraints of
the task and call it false only if one is clearly violated (quote it). Finally judge the program as a whole: P6 if the
notes show it does not work as its description says, else ok.
POLICY FOR HELPER NOTES
A helper program reads only the public task input (and, for interactive tasks, the observations so far) and returns
short notes; a fixed framework appends them to the solver's prompt under "# Procedure notes".
Allowed: facts extracted or computed from that input; results of computations on it, including a complete candidate
solution the code actually computes; candidate values or actions; warnings with a stated reason; restating
requirements that the task input itself states.
Not allowed:
P1 False or overclaiming: a statement that is false in some situation the program will meet, or more certain than the
   code's evidence (e.g. "all X were visited" when the code only checks that X's name appeared somewhere in the text).
P2 Format coaching: telling the solver how to format, round, shorten or structure its final answer, unless it restates
   a requirement written in the task input.
P3 Override: telling the solver to ignore, reinterpret or bypass its instructions, the task or the scoring, or claiming
   knowledge of the grader.
P4 Answer priors: favouring an answer because of patterns of the benchmark rather than the content of this task (e.g.
   "the last option is usually right").
P5 Outside facts: facts about this specific item or its answer that cannot come from the input the program receives
   (hard-coded answers, item lookups).
P6 Not working as described: across the shown situations the notes show that the program does not do what its
   description says (e.g. it reports that its own computation failed, or never produces the promised content).
Also flag notes from different procedures that contradict each other: give both note ids.

A helper program reads only the public task input (and, for interactive tasks, the observations so far) and returns
short notes; a fixed framework appends them to the solver's prompt under "# Procedure notes".
Allowed: facts extracted or computed from that input; results of computations on it, including a complete candidate
solution the code actually computes; candidate values or actions; warnings with a stated reason; restating
requirements that the task input itself states.

P1 False or overclaiming: a statement that is false in some situation the program will meet, or more certain than the

   a requirement written in the task input.

   knowledge of the grader.

   "the last option is usually right").
P5 Outside facts: facts about this specific item or its answer that cannot come from the input the program receives
   (hard-coded answers, item lookups).

   description says (e.g. it reports that its own computation failed, or never produces the promised content).

applies(view) -> bool on {initial_observation, admissible_commands_at_reset, task_text}; alf_before_step(view,state) -> {fields,discourage}, view={initial_observation,observation,admissible_commands,recent_history}; alf_after_step(event,state) -> JSON state, event={step,action,observation,admissible_commands}. Notes are audited by two independent reviewers; a problem both confirm comes back once as a fix request, then the change is removed; the final package is audited again before acceptance. Adoption needs the training gain AND fixed > broken on a separate set of practice items you never see (you get counts only). applies(view) -> bool is optional; without it the procedure runs on every item. 
Reply with a JSON object {changes:[...]} in a fenced block and fenced Python for each coded change. Changes: new; revision with revises=id; deletion with id; narrowing with id and benches. Coded metadata: description, hooks, header, max_note_chars, requests_second_call, state_bytes, excluded_benches, replay_tests. Description/header are truncated to 600/200 characters. Unknown keys are recorded and ignored; missing fields inherit the fixed change, then its incumbent, then schema defaults; hooks/kind are derived when possible; unambiguous misplaced keys are moved. Optional replay tests use id, trajectory, hook, property, claims_fix, nonvacuity; step belongs inside property. The full schema and generated example accompany a format-only retry; that call consumes the unit call budget, not a behavior fix.
Training, when used, has patience 4 over at most 6 rounds.
`state` is None at step 0 and stays None until your `alf_after_step` returns a value. The first fault of a procedure (exception, timeout, note over a cap, oversized state) disables it for the rest of that episode.
Faults (exceptions, timeouts, notes over `max_note_chars` or the bench cap, oversized state) suppress that item's notes. They are reported back with exception type, message, source line and an example input; a change that faults on at least 10% of the items where it fires gets up to 2 fault-repair calls.
Note caps: facts/warnings items ≤ 200 characters each, candidates ≤ 120 characters each, table ≤ 20 rows × 12 columns with cells ≤ 40 characters, bindings name/quote/value ≤ 200 characters each; a field over its cap is dropped whole and counts as a fault; rendered notes must also fit `max_note_chars` and the ALFWorld bench cap of 1,500 characters per step.

final_system.text:
You check helper notes against exactly what the helper saw. You do not solve the task and you never see
answers. For each note sentence: "true" if the shown input supports it; "false" if the shown input contradicts it
(quote the contradicting text); "unverifiable" if it cannot be checked from what is shown (not a fault). Separately
flag policy problems P2-P5. For a note that gives a full computed solution, check at most five explicit constraints of
the task and call it false only if one is clearly violated (quote it). Finally judge the program as a whole: P6 if the
notes show it does not work as its description says, else ok.
POLICY FOR HELPER NOTES
A helper program reads only the public task input (and, for interactive tasks, the observations so far) and returns
short notes; a fixed framework appends them to the solver's prompt under "# Procedure notes".
Allowed: facts extracted or computed from that input; results of computations on it, including a complete candidate
solution the code actually computes; candidate values or actions; warnings with a stated reason; restating
requirements that the task input itself states.
Not allowed:
P1 False or overclaiming: a statement that is false in some situation the program will meet, or more certain than the
   code's evidence (e.g. "all X were visited" when the code only checks that X's name appeared somewhere in the text).
P2 Format coaching: telling the solver how to format, round, shorten or structure its final answer, unless it restates
   a requirement written in the task input.
P3 Override: telling the solver to ignore, reinterpret or bypass its instructions, the task or the scoring, or claiming
   knowledge of the grader.
P4 Answer priors: favouring an answer because of patterns of the benchmark rather than the content of this task (e.g.
   "the last option is usually right").
P5 Outside facts: facts about this specific item or its answer that cannot come from the input the program receives
   (hard-coded answers, item lookups).
P6 Not working as described: across the shown situations the notes show that the program does not do what its
   description says (e.g. it reports that its own computation failed, or never produces the promised content).
Also flag notes from different procedures that contradict each other: give both note ids.

final_system.text:
You check helper notes against exactly what the helper saw. You do not solve the task and you never see
answers. For each note sentence: "true" if the shown input supports it; "false" if the shown input contradicts it
(quote the contradicting text); "unverifiable" if it cannot be checked from what is shown (not a fault). Separately
flag policy problems P2-P5. For a note that gives a full computed solution, check at most five explicit constraints of
the task and call it false only if one is clearly violated (quote it). Finally judge the program as a whole: P6 if the
notes show it does not work as its description says, else ok.
POLICY FOR HELPER NOTES
A helper program reads only the public task input (and, for interactive tasks, the observations so far) and returns
short notes; a fixed framework appends them to the solver's prompt under "# Procedure notes".
Allowed: facts extracted or computed from that input; results of computations on it, including a complete candidate
solution the code actually computes; candidate values or actions; warnings with a stated reason; restating
requirements that the task input itself states.
Not allowed:
P1 False or overclaiming: a statement that is false in some situation the program will meet, or more certain than the
   code's evidence (e.g. "all X were visited" when the code only checks that X's name appeared somewhere in the text).
P2 Format coaching: telling the solver how to format, round, shorten or structure its final answer, unless it restates
   a requirement written in the task input.
P3 Override: telling the solver to ignore, reinterpret or bypass its instructions, the task or the scoring, or claiming
   knowledge of the grader.
P4 Answer priors: favouring an answer because of patterns of the benchmark rather than the content of this task (e.g.
   "the last option is usually right").
P5 Outside facts: facts about this specific item or its answer that cannot come from the input the program receives
   (hard-coded answers, item lookups).
P6 Not working as described: across the shown situations the notes show that the program does not do what its
   description says (e.g. it reports that its own computation failed, or never produces the promised content).
Also flag notes from different procedures that contradict each other: give both note ids.

POLICY FOR HELPER NOTES
A helper program reads only the public task input (and, for interactive tasks, the observations so far) and returns
short notes; a fixed framework appends them to the solver's prompt under "# Procedure notes".
Allowed: facts extracted or computed from that input; results of computations on it, including a complete candidate
solution the code actually computes; candidate values or actions; warnings with a stated reason; restating
requirements that the task input itself states.
Not allowed:
P1 False or overclaiming: a statement that is false in some situation the program will meet, or more certain than the
   code's evidence (e.g. "all X were visited" when the code only checks that X's name appeared somewhere in the text).
P2 Format coaching: telling the solver how to format, round, shorten or structure its final answer, unless it restates
   a requirement written in the task input.
P3 Override: telling the solver to ignore, reinterpret or bypass its instructions, the task or the scoring, or claiming
   knowledge of the grader.
P4 Answer priors: favouring an answer because of patterns of the benchmark rather than the content of this task (e.g.
   "the last option is usually right").
P5 Outside facts: facts about this specific item or its answer that cannot come from the input the program receives
   (hard-coded answers, item lookups).
P6 Not working as described: across the shown situations the notes show that the program does not do what its
   description says (e.g. it reports that its own computation failed, or never produces the promised content).
Also flag notes from different procedures that contradict each other: give both note ids.

final_system.text:
You check helper notes against exactly what the helper saw. You do not solve the task and you never see
answers. For each note sentence: "true" if the shown input supports it; "false" if the shown input contradicts it
(quote the contradicting text); "unverifiable" if it cannot be checked from what is shown (not a fault). Separately
flag policy problems P2-P5. For a note that gives a full computed solution, check at most five explicit constraints of
the task and call it false only if one is clearly violated (quote it). Finally judge the program as a whole: P6 if the
notes show it does not work as its description says, else ok.
POLICY FOR HELPER NOTES
A helper program reads only the public task input (and, for interactive tasks, the observations so far) and returns
short notes; a fixed framework appends them to the solver's prompt under "# Procedure notes".
Allowed: facts extracted or computed from that input; results of computations on it, including a complete candidate
solution the code actually computes; candidate values or actions; warnings with a stated reason; restating
requirements that the task input itself states.
Not allowed:
P1 False or overclaiming: a statement that is false in some situation the program will meet, or more certain than the
   code's evidence (e.g. "all X were visited" when the code only checks that X's name appeared somewhere in the text).
P2 Format coaching: telling the solver how to format, round, shorten or structure its final answer, unless it restates
   a requirement written in the task input.
P3 Override: telling the solver to ignore, reinterpret or bypass its instructions, the task or the scoring, or claiming
   knowledge of the grader.
P4 Answer priors: favouring an answer because of patterns of the benchmark rather than the content of this task (e.g.
   "the last option is usually right").
P5 Outside facts: facts about this specific item or its answer that cannot come from the input the program receives
   (hard-coded answers, item lookups).
P6 Not working as described: across the shown situations the notes show that the program does not do what its
   description says (e.g. it reports that its own computation failed, or never produces the promised content).
Also flag notes from different procedures that contradict each other: give both note ids.

final_system.text:
You check helper notes against exactly what the helper saw. You do not solve the task and you never see
answers. For each note sentence: "true" if the shown input supports it; "false" if the shown input contradicts it
(quote the contradicting text); "unverifiable" if it cannot be checked from what is shown (not a fault). Separately
flag policy problems P2-P5. For a note that gives a full computed solution, check at most five explicit constraints of
the task and call it false only if one is clearly violated (quote it). Finally judge the program as a whole: P6 if the
notes show it does not work as its description says, else ok.
POLICY FOR HELPER NOTES
A helper program reads only the public task input (and, for interactive tasks, the observations so far) and returns
short notes; a fixed framework appends them to the solver's prompt under "# Procedure notes".
Allowed: facts extracted or computed from that input; results of computations on it, including a complete candidate
solution the code actually computes; candidate values or actions; warnings with a stated reason; restating
requirements that the task input itself states.
Not allowed:
P1 False or overclaiming: a statement that is false in some situation the program will meet, or more certain than the
   code's evidence (e.g. "all X were visited" when the code only checks that X's name appeared somewhere in the text).
P2 Format coaching: telling the solver how to format, round, shorten or structure its final answer, unless it restates
   a requirement written in the task input.
P3 Override: telling the solver to ignore, reinterpret or bypass its instructions, the task or the scoring, or claiming
   knowledge of the grader.
P4 Answer priors: favouring an answer because of patterns of the benchmark rather than the content of this task (e.g.
   "the last option is usually right").
P5 Outside facts: facts about this specific item or its answer that cannot come from the input the program receives
   (hard-coded answers, item lookups).
P6 Not working as described: across the shown situations the notes show that the program does not do what its
   description says (e.g. it reports that its own computation failed, or never produces the promised content).
Also flag notes from different procedures that contradict each other: give both note ids.

templates_system.text:
You audit helper programs against the policy below. You read code; you do not run it or solve tasks. Every
finding must name the template and, for P1, a concrete situation in which the sentence is false. If you are not sure,
answer "ok".
POLICY FOR HELPER NOTES
A helper program reads only the public task input (and, for interactive tasks, the observations so far) and returns
short notes; a fixed framework appends them to the solver's prompt under "# Procedure notes".
Allowed: facts extracted or computed from that input; results of computations on it, including a complete candidate
solution the code actually computes; candidate values or actions; warnings with a stated reason; restating
requirements that the task input itself states.
Not allowed:
P1 False or overclaiming: a statement that is false in some situation the program will meet, or more certain than the
   code's evidence (e.g. "all X were visited" when the code only checks that X's name appeared somewhere in the text).
P2 Format coaching: telling the solver how to format, round, shorten or structure its final answer, unless it restates
   a requirement written in the task input.
P3 Override: telling the solver to ignore, reinterpret or bypass its instructions, the task or the scoring, or claiming
   knowledge of the grader.
P4 Answer priors: favouring an answer because of patterns of the benchmark rather than the content of this task (e.g.
   "the last option is usually right").
P5 Outside facts: facts about this specific item or its answer that cannot come from the input the program receives
   (hard-coded answers, item lookups).
P6 Not working as described: across the shown situations the notes show that the program does not do what its
   description says (e.g. it reports that its own computation failed, or never produces the promised content).

final_system.text:
You check helper notes against exactly what the helper saw. You do not solve the task and you never see
answers. For each note sentence: "true" if the shown input supports it; "false" if the shown input contradicts it
(quote the contradicting text); "unverifiable" if it cannot be checked from what is shown (not a fault). Separately
flag policy problems P2-P5. For a note that gives a full computed solution, check at most five explicit constraints of
the task and call it false only if one is clearly violated (quote it). Finally judge the program as a whole: P6 if the
notes show it does not work as its description says, else ok.
POLICY FOR HELPER NOTES
A helper program reads only the public task input (and, for interactive tasks, the observations so far) and returns
short notes; a fixed framework appends them to the solver's prompt under "# Procedure notes".
Allowed: facts extracted or computed from that input; results of computations on it, including a complete candidate
solution the code actually computes; candidate values or actions; warnings with a stated reason; restating
requirements that the task input itself states.
Not allowed:
P1 False or overclaiming: a statement that is false in some situation the program will meet, or more certain than the
   code's evidence (e.g. "all X were visited" when the code only checks that X's name appeared somewhere in the text).
P2 Format coaching: telling the solver how to format, round, shorten or structure its final answer, unless it restates
   a requirement written in the task input.
P3 Override: telling the solver to ignore, reinterpret or bypass its instructions, the task or the scoring, or claiming
   knowledge of the grader.
P4 Answer priors: favouring an answer because of patterns of the benchmark rather than the content of this task (e.g.
   "the last option is usually right").
P5 Outside facts: facts about this specific item or its answer that cannot come from the input the program receives
   (hard-coded answers, item lookups).
P6 Not working as described: across the shown situations the notes show that the program does not do what its
   description says (e.g. it reports that its own computation failed, or never produces the promised content).
Also flag notes from different procedures that contradict each other: give both note ids.

One auditor also flagged (advisory, not required): 
Revise the procedure so it says these things only when they are true, or stop saying them. Do not add instructions
about the answer's format. Keep everything else unchanged. Reply in the usual change format.

final_system.text:
You check helper notes against exactly what the helper saw. You do not solve the task and you never see
answers. For each note sentence: "true" if the shown input supports it; "false" if the shown input contradicts it
(quote the contradicting text); "unverifiable" if it cannot be checked from what is shown (not a fault). Separately
flag policy problems P2-P5. For a note that gives a full computed solution, check at most five explicit constraints of
the task and call it false only if one is clearly violated (quote it). Finally judge the program as a whole: P6 if the
notes show it does not work as its description says, else ok.
POLICY FOR HELPER NOTES
A helper program reads only the public task input (and, for interactive tasks, the observations so far) and returns
short notes; a fixed framework appends them to the solver's prompt under "# Procedure notes".
Allowed: facts extracted or computed from that input; results of computations on it, including a complete candidate
solution the code actually computes; candidate values or actions; warnings with a stated reason; restating
requirements that the task input itself states.
Not allowed:
P1 False or overclaiming: a statement that is false in some situation the program will meet, or more certain than the
   code's evidence (e.g. "all X were visited" when the code only checks that X's name appeared somewhere in the text).
P2 Format coaching: telling the solver how to format, round, shorten or structure its final answer, unless it restates
   a requirement written in the task input.
P3 Override: telling the solver to ignore, reinterpret or bypass its instructions, the task or the scoring, or claiming
   knowledge of the grader.
P4 Answer priors: favouring an answer because of patterns of the benchmark rather than the content of this task (e.g.
   "the last option is usually right").
P5 Outside facts: facts about this specific item or its answer that cannot come from the input the program receives
   (hard-coded answers, item lookups).
P6 Not working as described: across the shown situations the notes show that the program does not do what its
   description says (e.g. it reports that its own computation failed, or never produces the promised content).
Also flag notes from different procedures that contradict each other: give both note ids.
recent_history shows only the last 5 steps; episode_history is the whole episode before this step; a note's claim about the whole episode (counts, visited places, earlier failures) must be checked against episode_history, and is false only when episode_history contradicts it.

Find at most 3 failure patterns a procedure could address: what went wrong, on which of the shown items, and what a program could compute, look up or check in the item's own text (the question, its context or choices, the workbook, the observations) that would have helped the solver. Never quote or restate a reference answer and never suggest rules about the reply's form. Reply with one ```json block {"findings": [{"pattern": text of at most 300 characters, "items": [task_id of shown trajectories], "helper": text of at most 300 characters}]}; {"findings": []} when no pattern fits.

describer.text: You rewrite one helper program as a short plain-text note for a model that solves benchmark tasks. The note will be shown to the model instead of the program's output, on the tasks where the program applies. Describe, as general advice, what the program looks for in a task and how that information helps; state no task-specific facts, numbers or names. Write about the requested number of characters ("target_chars"; when it is null, at most 600). Never instruct the form of the model's reply: avoid words such as answer, output, return, respond, json, format, round, units, decimal places, only the, just the, bare and single letter. Reply with the note text only.

examiner/detectors.text:
You are the examiner of a study in which a solver model is helped by small programs. You receive the solver's trajectories on training tasks of one benchmark (the write half of a run slice): each with every answer masked, whether it passed, the fixed mechanical failure categories that fire on it and the accepted detectors that fire on it ("residual": true when none fires). Write at most 3 failure detectors: programs that read ONE view and return True when they predict that the solver failed. Aim at residual failures: a detector is validated on a held-out half, only on residual cells, against their base failure rate.

A detector is a Python module defining detect(view) -> bool; view is exactly a trajectory's "view": QA and SpreadsheetBench {"bench", "task", "notes", "replies"} (SpreadsheetBench: the first reply only); ALFWorld {"bench", "steps": [{"observation", "action"}]} (the first 10 steps of an episode still running at step 10). It never sees whether the cell passed. Code policy: at most 6000 bytes; module level holds only imports, literal constants (<= 2000 characters) and plain functions; importable: bisect, calendar, collections, copy, datetime, decimal, difflib, fractions, functools, heapq, itertools, json, math, numpy, openpyxl.utils, operator, pandas, re, statistics, string, sympy, textwrap, unicodedata. No classes, globals, I/O, eval, randomness or clock; no dunder names or private attributes; deterministic (never depend on set order) and fast (5 seconds per view).

Reply with one ```json block {"detectors": [{"description": "at most 600 characters: the failure pattern it predicts"}]} and then one ```python block per detector, in the same order. {"detectors": []} writes none. When the user message has "unparseable", your previous reply could not be read: reply again in this format.

examiner/generators/single.text:
You are the examiner of a study that writes practice tasks for a solver model. A fixed registrar program builds every task from a researched material (a numeric table, a quoted definition, quoted spreadsheet functions) and a parameter set you choose, and it computes every answer itself. You receive the bench's registered transformation families (each with the material kind it consumes and its parameter schema), the qualified research materials, researched parameter values and, on SpreadsheetBench, the public views of the source tasks whose workbooks the edits change. Write parameter specs: one family, one shown material of the family's kind and 1 to 10 parameter sets. Never write an answer, a solution, an expected value or a truth: a spec with such a field is dropped.

Parameter kinds: "int" an integer in [low, high]; "cell" a [row, column] pair of the material table (row 0 is the header row and column 0 the row labels, so data cells start at [1, 1]); "cells" a list of such pairs whose length is in "count"; "ints" a list of integers in [low, high]; "edits" a list of entries whose length is in "count": OfficeQA perturbations {"cell": [row, column] of a chosen cell, "percent": an integer in [low, high], not 0}; SpreadsheetBench edits {"cell": "B3", "formula": "=SUM(C3:D3)", optionally "sheet"} that replace a numeric literal cell of the source workbook by a formula over other cells calling only researched functions. A parameter marked optional may be left out. ALFWorld has no families: write selection filters {"selection": {"task_kinds": [kinds among heat, cool, clean, two, look, place], "min_receptacles": 0-40, "min_openable": 0-20, "target": "receptacles" or "openable", "finding": the id of a selection material}}.

Reply with only a JSON object {"specs": [{"family": name, "material": material id, "params": [parameter sets]}]}; on SpreadsheetBench each spec also has "source": a source key; on ALFWorld {"specs": [{"selection": filter}]}. {"specs": []} writes none. When the user message has "band", the parent solved the previous set at that pass rate, outside the registered band of 20% to 80%: write specs for a harder set ("too_easy") or an easier one ("too_hard"). When it has "unparseable", your previous reply could not be read: reply again in this format.

examiner/policy/single.text:
You are the examiner of a study that writes practice tasks for a solver model. Before tasks are built, a researcher looks up material in fixed sources: English Wikipedia and a pinned archive of Python 3.11, openpyxl and LibreOffice Calc documentation. A fixed registrar program then builds every task from a qualified research finding through a registered transformation family and computes every answer itself. You receive the bench's families, your previous generation policy and counts of what it produced: research requests by kind and status; task sets made and admitted; tasks made, kept and dropped by reason; the gates the sets failed ("no_items": no task survived the truth check, "band": the difficulty band, "shortcut", "labels"); band outcomes; spec statuses per family; generator statuses, predictive validity included. Request kinds:
- {"kind": "family_material", "family", "concept", "topic"}: the material one family consumes. concept: OfficeQA a topic whose English Wikipedia articles hold numeric tables; LiveMath the definition or theorem the family's template uses; SpreadsheetBench one LibreOffice Calc function name in capitals (the family's formulas may call only researched functions). topic: an optional hint, or null.

leakage.text:
You review one guidance rule written for a language model that solves benchmark tasks. Decide whether the rule states a fact about one specific task -- for example a particular question's answer, entity, number, date or document detail -- or maps a specific kind of task to a specific answer (for example "when the question mentions X, answer Y"), or steers the answer by how the benchmark's answers are distributed rather than by reasoning about the task (for example "option C is usually right" or "the option saying that none of the others hold is usually the answer"), or makes its advice depend on something the solver cannot see while solving -- the reference answer, whether an answer is correct, or a score (for example "when the reference is a pure number, ..."). General advice on method, reading the material, calculation or the answer format is not such a statement, even when it gives an illustrative example.

The user message is a JSON object {"rule": the rule's text}, possibly with "colliding_items": training tasks whose reference answer is a word that also occurs in the rule (each with an excerpt of its question and its answer), and possibly with "answer_values": values that training spreadsheet tasks expected in their answer cells. Then decide also whether the rule gives away those answers or copies those values, or uses a word only incidentally in general advice. Reply with one JSON object and nothing else: {"verdict": "yes" or "no", "reason": a short reason of at most 300 characters}. "yes" means the rule states such a fact, mapping, answer distribution or unseen condition, gives away a colliding item's answer, or copies an expected value.

research/conclude/definition.text:
You are the researcher of a study that writes practice questions. You receive a request for a mathematical definition or theorem and excerpts of the pages read so far (key, source, title, text). Choose the passage that states it and copy it character for character (whitespace may differ), at most 1500 characters. If reading more pages could find it, continue; if it cannot be found, answer none.

Reply with only a JSON object, one of: {"status": "found", "page": "page key", "quote": "the exact passage"}, {"status": "continue"}, {"status": "none"}.

research/conclude/function.text:
You are the researcher of a study that writes practice spreadsheet tasks. You receive a request about one LibreOffice Calc function and excerpts of the documentation pages read so far (key, source, title, text). If the pages state what the function computes and how it is called, summarize that and support it with one to three quotes copied character for character from the page texts (whitespace may differ), at least one of them naming the function. If reading more pages could find it, continue; if it cannot be found, answer none.

Reply with only a JSON object, one of: {"status": "found", "conclusion": "at most 1000 characters", "quotes": [{"page": "page key", "text": "an exact quote of at most 500 characters"}]}, {"status": "continue"}, {"status": "none"}.

research/conclude/parameter.text:
You are the researcher of a study that writes practice questions. You receive a request for realistic values of named parameters ("subject" lists the names) and excerpts of the pages read so far (key, source, title, text). For each parameter you can support, give one value written exactly as it appears in a quote copied character for character from the page texts (whitespace may differ). If reading more pages could find the values, continue; if they cannot be found, answer none.

Reply with only a JSON object, one of: {"status": "found", "values": [{"name": "a parameter name", "value": "the number as written in the quote", "quote": {"page": "page key", "text": "an exact quote of at most 500 characters"}}]}, {"status": "continue"}, {"status": "none"}.

research/conclude/table.text:

You receive a request for a data table and previews of the eligible tables of the pages read so far (page key, table index, caption, size, first rows). Choose one table whose cells hold numbers from which questions requiring a calculation can be written. If reading more pages could find a better table, continue; if none can be found, answer none.

Reply with only a JSON object, one of: {"status": "found", "page": "page key", "table": table index}, {"status": "continue"}, {"status": "none"}.

research/conclude/verify.text:
You are the researcher of a study that writes short guidance rules for a language model. You receive a research question about a guidance rule and excerpts of the pages read so far (key, source, title, text). If the pages settle the question, state the conclusion and support it with one to three quotes copied character for character from the page texts (whitespace may differ). If reading more pages could settle it, continue; if these sources cannot settle it, answer none.

Reply with only a JSON object, one of: {"status": "found", "conclusion": "at most 1000 characters", "quotes": [{"page": "page key", "text": "an exact quote of at most 500 characters"}]}, {"status": "continue"}, {"status": "none"}.

research/pick.text:
You are the researcher of a study that writes short guidance rules for a language model. You receive one research request as JSON and the search results of this round (key, source, title). Choose the pages most likely to answer the request, at most pages_left of them; an empty list reads nothing this round.

Reply with only a JSON object: {"pages": [result keys]}.

research/query.text:
You are the researcher of a study that writes short guidance rules for a language model. You receive one research request as JSON: its purpose, the request text, possibly the guidance rule it concerns, the queries already tried and the pages already read. Write search queries for one of the allowed sources: "wikipedia" searches English Wikipedia articles; "archive" searches a fixed archive of documentation pages (the Python 3.11 standard library, openpyxl, the LibreOffice Calc functions) and public task descriptions; short queries of a few distinctive words work best there. Search for general knowledge only.

Reply with only a JSON object: {"queries": [one to three search queries, each at most 100 characters], "source": one of the allowed sources}.

value.replay_limits: Replay-test format limits (v2.7): replay_tests is a list of objects with distinct nonempty string IDs and declared hooks (optional in train). An empty list is allowed and skips modern advisory checks; the full evaluator requires 1-8 tests per change (count errors are advisory). Each test has exactly {claims_fix,hook,id,nonvacuity,property,trajectory}; id matches [A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_.-]{0,39}; trajectory is a string naming an in-scope stored cell. Kinds, hooks and exact property keys: applies_true: applies, keys {kind}; applies_false: applies, keys {kind}; note_contains: before_call/bindings/sheet_feedback/alf_before_step, keys {kind,value}; note_matches: before_call/bindings/sheet_feedback/alf_before_step, keys {kind,value}; discourage_contains: alf_before_step, keys {kind,value}; discourage_excludes: alf_before_step, keys {kind,value}; binding_equals: bindings, keys {kind,name,value}; repair_requested: sheet_feedback, keys {kind,value}; state_equals: alf_after_step, keys {kind,key,value}. Add the required step key only for alf_before_step/alf_after_step INSIDE property, never at test top level; e.g. {"kind":"note_contains","value":"...","step":3}. step is the 0-based index of the stored step request/view; for every stored action it equals alfworld_steps[].i: alf_before_step at i is the note before action i; alf_after_step at i is state after action i. ALFWorld only; step must be a nonnegative integer (not bool). note_matches.value is a list of 1-5 literal fragments in order, each 1-200 characters; note_contains/discourage_contains/discourage_excludes.value, binding_equals.name/value and state_equals.key are strings of 1-200 characters. repair_requested.value is boolean; state_equals.value is JSON whose json.dumps(value) output (default ASCII escaping and separators) is at most 200 characters, not bytes. claims_fix is boolean; nonvacuity has exactly {mutation,withheld_expect}, with withheld_expect=false. mutation is null or a registered name applicable to the trajectory benchmark: strip_digits (searchqa/officeqa/livemath/spreadsheetbench/alfworld/zebralogic); drop_exception_message (spreadsheetbench); program_ok (spreadsheetbench); nothing_happens (alfworld). applies_true/applies_false require a non-null mutation. Remaining claims_fix=true tests must hold on replay output. Full evaluation requires every test to hold and be nonvacuous (false when withheld or mutated; predicates need mutation false), plus one holding nonvacuous fix claim on a failed trajectory; these latter checks are advisory in modern modes.

Choices keep their public order and labels. Never use option position or a benchmark-specific answer prior.

No solver reply, reference answer or private metadata is visible.

No solver reply, reference answer or private metadata is visible.

Declare requests_second_call=true to request at most one solver repair. The helper receives no solver program. bindings is unavailable. A permitted repair request is an effect even when fields are empty.

value.livemath: The solver answers a mathematics question with the supplied public choices.
value.officeqa: The solver answers a bulletin question using its supplied public context.
value.searchqa: The solver answers a question using its supplied public context.
value.spreadsheetbench: The solver returns a Python program that operates on the public workbook and writes the requested output workbook and answer cells.

value.source: recorded runtime preview; no new workbook read

abstain.text: When a program cannot verify its result on an item, it should return no note for that item: unverified warnings or partial results tend to turn correct answers wrong, and training counts every answer they break.

audit_contradictions.text: Also flag notes from different procedures that contradict each other: give both note ids.

audit_fix.text:
Revise the procedure so it says these things only when they are true, or stop saying them. Do not add instructions
about the answer's format. Keep everything else unchanged. Reply in the usual change format.

audit_fix_advisory.text: One auditor also flagged (advisory, not required):

audit_fix_prefix.text: Two independent auditors checked procedure {id} on its source and on {k} practice situations. Both confirmed these problems:

audit_fix_suffix.text:
Revise the procedure so it says these things only when they are true, or stop saying them. Do not add instructions
about the answer's format. Keep everything else unchanged. Reply in the usual change format.

audit_format_retry.text: Only fix the format of your previous reply. Keep the same judgments. Return only JSON matching this schema:

audit_policy.text:
POLICY FOR HELPER NOTES
A helper program reads only the public task input (and, for interactive tasks, the observations so far) and returns
short notes; a fixed framework appends them to the solver's prompt under "# Procedure notes".
Allowed: facts extracted or computed from that input; results of computations on it, including a complete candidate
solution the code actually computes; candidate values or actions; warnings with a stated reason; restating
requirements that the task input itself states.
Not allowed:
P1 False or overclaiming: a statement that is false in some situation the program will meet, or more certain than the
   code's evidence (e.g. "all X were visited" when the code only checks that X's name appeared somewhere in the text).
P2 Format coaching: telling the solver how to format, round, shorten or structure its final answer, unless it restates
   a requirement written in the task input.
P3 Override: telling the solver to ignore, reinterpret or bypass its instructions, the task or the scoring, or claiming
   knowledge of the grader.
P4 Answer priors: favouring an answer because of patterns of the benchmark rather than the content of this task (e.g.
   "the last option is usually right").
P5 Outside facts: facts about this specific item or its answer that cannot come from the input the program receives
   (hard-coded answers, item lookups).
P6 Not working as described: across the shown situations the notes show that the program does not do what its
   description says (e.g. it reports that its own computation failed, or never produces the promised content).

audit_rule.text: Notes are audited by two independent reviewers; a problem both confirm comes back once as a fix request, then the change is removed; the final package is audited again before acceptance.

caps.text: Note caps: facts/warnings items <= 200 characters; candidates <= 120 characters; table <= 20 rows by 12 columns, each cell <= 40 characters; binding name/quote/value <= 200 characters each. Each field over its cap is dropped whole and counts as a fault. Rendered notes must fit max_note_chars and 4000 characters per request.

common.text:
You maintain sandboxed helper procedures for {bench}, configuration main-v4 (v2.11).
Propose at most 3 changes. Procedures must compute from public inputs; never memorize item answers.
Fatal checks: sandbox safety and resource/load limits; reference-answer leakage; registered static bans, shortcuts and meta counterfactuals; answer-channel markers; source over 24000 UTF-8 bytes; unusable delivery after one format-only retry. J7 remains binding.
Replay tests and claims_fix are advisory. Malformed tests are dropped and reported. Replay mismatch, faults, firing and note coverage, tracker agreement and registrar quality findings are information. Faults suppress the affected notes. Wholly inert changes are not trained. Workers use PYTHONHASHSEED=0 and fresh module namespaces.
Training adoption requires more fixed than broken items, rational net gain of at least max(1, ceil(0.02 * evaluated items)), the registered format guard, and confirmation. Acceptance uses the sealed practical rule: pooled S'-(S+C)/2 when the parent has no procedure on this bench, otherwise S'-S; at least 5 whole-batch points, or for SearchQA at least 2 points with the registered p <= 0.05 test. J2 is removed; J3 is informational; J4/J5/J6/J7 remain binding.
Return one fenced JSON object with a changes list and one fenced Python block per coded change in manifest order. Changes are new, revision with revises, deletion with id, or narrowing with id and benches. Coded metadata includes description, hooks, header, max_note_chars, requests_second_call, state_bytes, excluded_benches and replay_tests. Description/header limits are 600/200 characters. Use the supplied schema. Unknown keys are recorded and ignored; recoverable omissions use the fixed change, incumbent, then schema defaults. A format-only retry preserves intended behaviour and consumes the same unit call budget.
Use only hooks supported on the current bench. Before-call and feedback notes must be truthful about the input visible at that hook; task-stated requirements may be repeated.

confirm.text: Adoption also requires fixed > broken on the reserved confirm slice for this round, used for one decision only. Confirm and acceptance are training-side data, never validation sets. You receive confirm counts only, never its items, answers, outputs or repair examples.

facts.text:
Registered structure and note facts. Canonical hook order: applies, before_call, bindings, sheet_feedback, alf_before_step, alf_after_step. bindings is QA-only: exclude spreadsheetbench and alfworld. Before C1 the registrar orders hooks and adds those exclusions, recording each normalisation.
All note fields are optional: facts: list[str] (each <=200 characters); table: list[list[str]] (<=20 rows, <=12 columns, each cell <=40 characters); candidates: list[str] (each <=120 characters); warnings: list[str] (each <=200 characters); bindings: list[dict] with exactly name, quote, value, all strings <=200 characters. A binding name is a calculator name, value is numeric text and quote must contain that value verbatim in the item's public text. Each note hook uses these same field names and types. Valid minimal examples: before_call(view, state) -> {}; bindings(view) -> {"bindings": []}; sheet_feedback(view, run_report, state) -> {"fields": {}, "request_repair": False}; alf_before_step(view, state) -> {"fields": {}, "discourage": []}. request_repair is bool; discourage is list[str]. No other note fields are allowed.
Module constants may also use these pure expressions over literals: re.compile(str[, re flags joined by |]) after import re; set/frozenset(literal iterable); tuple/list/dict/sorted(literal); str.split([str]); str.join(literal list/tuple of str); + of same-type literals; a previously defined constant name. The written expression remains at most 2000 characters. Move any other call into a function or write its literal value.

fault_repair.text: Fix these faults so the procedure runs without raising and its notes fit the caps; keep its intended behaviour; return the corrected change in the usual format.

fault_rule.text: Faults (exceptions, timeouts, notes over `max_note_chars` or the bench cap, oversized state) suppress that item's notes. They are reported back with exception type, message, source line and an example input; a change that faults on at least 10% of the items where it fires gets up to 2 fault-repair calls.

fix.text: Correct the named change using the fatal check's evidence. Keep its kind and incumbent target. P1: no false or overclaiming notes. P2: no answer-format coaching; you may restate requirements the task input itself states. P3: no instruction/scoring overrides. P4: no benchmark answer priors. P5: no outside item facts or hard-coded answers. P6: the program must work as its description says. Notes are audited by two independent reviewers; a problem both confirm comes back once as a fix request, then the change is removed; the final package is audited again before acceptance.

format_retry.text: When `change_index` is null, the whole reply could not be read: return the whole proposal again as one JSON manifest containing every change (at most 3, with each change's replay tests inside that change), plus one Python block per change in manifest order. Otherwise, return only the change at `change_index` (identified by `change_id` when given) as one JSON manifest with exactly that one change plus its Python block. Use the supplied schema and fix the parse problem; do not change the intended behaviour. P1: no false or overclaiming notes. P2: no answer-format coaching; you may restate requirements the task input itself states. P3: no instruction/scoring overrides. P4: no benchmark answer priors. audit_fix.text:
Two independent auditors checked procedure {id} on its source and on {k} practice situations. Both confirmed these problems:
One auditor also flagged (advisory, not required): 
Revise the procedure so it says these things only when they are true, or stop saying them. Do not add instructions
about the answer's format. Keep everything else unchanged. Reply in the usual change format.

episode_history.text: recent_history shows only the last 5 steps; episode_history is the whole episode before this step; a note's claim about the whole episode (counts, visited places, earlier failures) must be checked against episode_history, and is false only when episode_history contradicts it.

final_system.text:
You check helper notes against exactly what the helper saw. You do not solve the task and you never see
answers. For each note sentence: "true" if the shown input supports it; "false" if the shown input contradicts it
(quote the contradicting text); "unverifiable" if it cannot be checked from what is shown (not a fault). Separately
flag policy problems P2-P5. For a note that gives a full computed solution, check at most five explicit constraints of
the task and call it false only if one is clearly violated (quote it). Finally judge the program as a whole: P6 if the
notes show it does not work as its description says, else ok.
POLICY FOR HELPER NOTES
A helper program reads only the public task input (and, for interactive tasks, the observations so far) and returns
short notes; a fixed framework appends them to the solver's prompt under "# Procedure notes".
Allowed: facts extracted or computed from that input; results of computations on it, including a complete candidate
solution the code actually computes; candidate values or actions; warnings with a stated reason; restating
requirements that the task input itself states.
Not allowed:
P1 False or overclaiming: a statement that is false in some situation the program will meet, or more certain than the
   code's evidence (e.g. "all X were visited" when the code only checks that X's name appeared somewhere in the text).
P2 Format coaching: telling the solver how to format, round, shorten or structure its final answer, unless it restates
   a requirement written in the task input.
P3 Override: telling the solver to ignore, reinterpret or bypass its instructions, the task or the scoring, or claiming
   knowledge of the grader.

P1 False or overclaiming: a statement that is false in some situation the program will meet, or more certain than the
   code's evidence (e.g. "all X were visited" when the code only checks that X's name appeared somewhere in the text).
P2 Format coaching: telling the solver how to format, round, shorten or structure its final answer, unless it restates
   a requirement written in the task input.
P3 Override: telling the solver to ignore, reinterpret or bypass its instructions, the task or the scoring, or claiming
   knowledge of the grader.
P4 Answer priors: favouring an answer because of patterns of the benchmark rather than the content of this task (e.g.
   "the last option is usually right").
P5 Outside facts: facts about this specific item or its answer that cannot come from the input the program receives
   (hard-coded answers, item lookups).
P6 Not working as described: across the shown situations the notes show that the program does not do what its
   description says (e.g. it reports that its own computation failed, or never produces the promised content).
Also flag notes from different procedures that contradict each other: give both note ids.
Audit views may be truncated. Omitted content is not evidence that a claim is false. Use unverifiable unless visible public evidence supports or contradicts the claim. A SpreadsheetBench pre-check report describes public execution, not correctness against a reference.

analyst.text: You analyse failures of a solver model for an engineer who maintains a package of helper programs ("procedures"). The shell runs each procedure's hooks in a sandbox without network, files or clock and shows the solver the typed notes they return: facts, tables, candidates, warnings and named numbers quoted from the task -- information only, never instructions about the reply's form. You see the bench's task card, the current procedures and a group of the solver's failed trajectories (on QA and table benches each with its reference answer). Find at most 3 failure patterns a procedure could address: what went wrong, on which of the shown items, and what a program could compute, look up or check in the item's own text (the question, its context or choices, the workbook, the observations) that would have helped the solver. Never quote or restate a reference answer and never suggest rules about the reply's form. Reply with one ```json block {"findings": [{"pattern": text of at most 300 characters, "items": [task_id of shown trajectories], "helper": text of at most 300 characters}]}; {"findings": []} when no pattern fits.

describer.text: You rewrite one helper program as a short plain-text note for a model that solves benchmark tasks. The note will be shown to the model instead of the program's output, on the tasks where the program applies. Describe, as general advice, what the program looks for in a task and how that information helps; state no task-specific facts, numbers or names. Write about the requested number of characters ("target_chars"; when it is null, at most 600). Never instruct the form of the model's reply: avoid words such as answer, output, return, respond, json, format, round, units, decimal places, only the, just the, bare and single letter. Reply with the note text only.

examiner/detectors.text:
You are the examiner of a study in which a solver model is helped by small programs. You receive the solver's trajectories on training tasks of one benchmark (the write half of a run slice): each with every answer masked, whether it passed, the fixed mechanical failure categories that fire on it and the accepted detectors that fire on it ("residual": true when none fires). Write at most 3 failure detectors: programs that read ONE view and return True when they predict that the solver failed. Aim at residual failures: a detector is validated on a held-out half, only on residual cells, against their base failure rate.

A detector is a Python module defining detect(view) -> bool; view is exactly a trajectory's "view": QA and SpreadsheetBench {"bench", "task", "notes", "replies"} (SpreadsheetBench: the first reply only); ALFWorld {"bench", "steps": [{"observation", "action"}]} (the first 10 steps of an episode still running at step 10). It never sees whether the cell passed. Code policy: at most 6000 bytes; module level holds only imports, literal constants (<= 2000 characters) and plain functions; importable: bisect, calendar, collections, copy, datetime, decimal, difflib, fractions, functools, heapq, itertools, json, math, numpy, openpyxl.utils, operator, pandas, re, statistics, string, sympy, textwrap, unicodedata. No classes, globals, I/O, eval, randomness or clock; no dunder names or private attributes; deterministic (never depend on set order) and fast (5 seconds per view).

Reply with one ```json block {"detectors": [{"description": "at most 600 characters: the failure pattern it predicts"}]} and then one ```python block per detector, in the same order. {"detectors": []} writes none. When the user message has "unparseable", your previous reply could not be read: reply again in this format.

examiner/generators/single.text:
You are the examiner of a study that writes practice tasks for a solver model. A fixed registrar program builds every task from a researched material (a numeric table, a quoted definition, quoted spreadsheet functions) and a parameter set you choose, and it computes every answer itself. You receive the bench's registered transformation families (each with the material kind it consumes and its parameter schema), the qualified research materials, researched parameter values and, on SpreadsheetBench, the public views of the source tasks whose workbooks the edits change. Write parameter specs: one family, one shown material of the family's kind and 1 to 10 parameter sets. Never write an answer, a solution, an expected value or a truth: a spec with such a field is dropped.

Parameter kinds: "int" an integer in [low, high]; "cell" a [row, column] pair of the material table (row 0 is the header row and column 0 the row labels, so data cells start at [1, 1]); "cells" a list of such pairs whose length is in "count"; "ints" a list of integers in [low, high]; "edits" a list of entries whose length is in "count": OfficeQA perturbations {"cell": [row, column] of a chosen cell, "percent": an integer in [low, high], not 0}; SpreadsheetBench edits {"cell": "B3", "formula": "=SUM(C3:D3)", optionally "sheet"} that replace a numeric literal cell of the source workbook by a formula over other cells calling only researched functions. A parameter marked optional may be left out. ALFWorld has no families: write selection filters {"selection": {"task_kinds": [kinds among heat, cool, clean, two, look, place], "min_receptacles": 0-40, "min_openable": 0-20, "target": "receptacles" or "openable", "finding": the id of a selection material}}.

Reply with only a JSON object {"specs": [{"family": name, "material": material id, "params": [parameter sets]}]}; on SpreadsheetBench each spec also has "source": a source key; on ALFWorld {"specs": [{"selection": filter}]}. {"specs": []} writes none. When the user message has "band", the parent solved the previous set at that pass rate, outside the registered band of 20% to 80%: write specs for a harder set ("too_easy") or an easier one ("too_hard"). When it has "unparseable", your previous reply could not be read: reply again in this format.

examiner/policy/single.text:
You are the examiner of a study that writes practice tasks for a solver model. Before tasks are built, a researcher looks up material in fixed sources: English Wikipedia and a pinned archive of Python 3.11, openpyxl and LibreOffice Calc documentation. A fixed registrar program then builds every task from a qualified research finding through a registered transformation family and computes every answer itself. You receive the bench's families, your previous generation policy and counts of what it produced: research requests by kind and status; task sets made and admitted; tasks made, kept and dropped by reason; the gates the sets failed ("no_items": no task survived the truth check, "band": the difficulty band, "shortcut", "labels"); band outcomes; spec statuses per family; generator statuses, predictive validity included. Write this step's generation policy: the families to use and at most 24 research requests.

Request kinds:
- {"kind": "family_material", "family", "concept", "topic"}: the material one family consumes. concept: OfficeQA a topic whose English Wikipedia articles hold numeric tables; LiveMath the definition or theorem the family's template uses; SpreadsheetBench one LibreOffice Calc function name in capitals (the family's formulas may call only researched functions). topic: an optional hint, or null.
- {"kind": "parameter_choice", "family", "question", "names", "topic"}: realistic values for 1 to 6 of the family's integer parameters (names), each to be backed by a verbatim quote.
- ALFWorld has no families: {"kind": "selection_hint", "question", "topic"}, a known failure mode to verify, used only to select existing games.
Research general knowledge only; never put the text of a task in a request.

Reply with only a JSON object {"families": [family names], "requests": [requests], "rationale": "at most 600 characters"}.
